title: Timberwolves Bench Depth Grades: Beringer, Dosunmu
text:
Timberwolves Bench Depth Grades: Beringer, Dosunmu — TWolves Blog 
 Skip to content TWOLVES BLOG Timberwolves Game Coverage Daily Howl Lynx Injury Report Schedules Wolvespedia Timberwolves The Break-Glass Test: Grading the Wolves Bench
 Preseason warned the Wolves had no break-glass big behind Gobert. We grade Beringer, Dosunmu, Shannon and Hyland from the 131-106 opener in Miami.
 Katie Walsh October 22, 2026 · 4 min read Minnesota opened the season by running Miami off the floor , 131-106, and the first live look at its most-questioned unit came back encouraging and nearly meaningless in the same breath.
 The preseason alarm was specific. Camp coverage kept circling the same hole in this Timberwolves roster: almost nothing proven behind Rudy Gobert . That SI breakdown laid out a short list: Trey Lyles for traditional frontcourt minutes, the foul-prone 19-year-old Joan Beringer as the young backup center, and two-way man Rocco Zikarsky as the nominal “break glass in case of emergency” option, probably bound for the G League. That was the worry the box score was supposed to address, so let’s grade the reserves against it, with one honest caveat stapled to every grade.
 The caveat: this was one blowout, and not an especially instructive one. Anthony Edwards hit nine threes on his way to 45 , the kind of eruption that turns any opponent into a cadaver by the third quarter. This wasn’t a depleted Heat team handing out minutes. It was a whole one, Bam Adebayo and a 35-point Giannis Antetokounmpo debut included, that simply got buried, which means a slice of these reserve minutes arrived after the result was settled.
 Start with the reserve who looked most ready, because it isn’t the one the thesis was about. Ayo Dosunmu went for 16 points on 6-of-13 with five rebounds and three assists in 29 minutes , and he played them like a sixth starter rather than a bench flier. He steadied the non-Edwards minutes, got downhill, defended two spots. The catch for the depth thesis is that Dosunmu is a guard. He answers the question of who stabilizes the second unit, not the question of who plays center when Gobert sits or tweaks something. Those are different holes.
 Which brings us to Beringer, the actual subject of the alarm. His line reads like nothing: 13 minutes, zero points on 0-of-2, one assist. Read the rebound column and it reads like the answer to the exact question being asked. Six boards, four offensive, in those 13 minutes, inside a team night that produced 17 offensive rebounds and 20 second-chance points. The specific fear was that Minnesota would get bullied on the glass the second Gobert left the floor. Beringer did the bullying instead. He also picked up a single foul, which matters, because his foul trouble is the one well-documented flaw everyone agreed would govern how long he could stay on the floor.
 I went back through all 13 of those minutes looking for the possession where Miami tried to post him up and make him pay for being young and new. It never came.
 Beringer looked most ready on the axis that actually scared everyone, rebounding and physicality, and least tested on everything else. A Heat team content to settle for jumpers never asked him to wall off a real roll man or manufacture a bucket the offense needed. Encouraging, genuinely. Proven, not close.
 Terrence Shannon Jr. is the one who should give you pause. Ten points looks fine until the shot chart loads: 3-of-9 from the floor, 2-of-7 from three, the last two scrounged at the line, in 20 minutes. Shannon’s problem has always been shot selection, not athleticism, and a 2-for-7 night from deep in a 25-point win is the version of him a playoff rotation can’t carry.
 Bones Hyland barely registered: 3:51, one three, then a seat. In a blowout with garbage time to spare, a guard fighting for rotation minutes getting under four of them is its own quiet verdict. You can’t grade a non-sample, but you can notice who Finch trusted when the game loosened and who he left on the bench.
 Did Finch address the bench specifically afterward? Not really. His postgame credit went to Jonathan Kuminga’s defense on Antetokounmpo (“He just wasn’t afraid to put his body on him continually”) and to the team’s conditioning. The backup-big question he had leaned on all week went unmentioned, which is its own small tell. You don’t declare a problem solved on the back of one cakewalk, and the most defensible interpretation of this bench is still the honest, middle-case one .
 So grade it straight. Most ready: Dosunmu, and it isn’t close, even if he doesn’t patch the hole the thesis cared about. Least ready: Shannon by shot selection, with Hyland incomplete because he never got on the floor. Beringer, the one it was all about, split the difference, the same way this bench stole a preseason night from these same Heat . He answered the narrow question and left the hard one for an opponent that actually tries.
 The emergency big looked fine on a night nobody pulled the alarm.
